content.title: Identifying Design Flaws and Confounding Variables
content.overview: This lesson focuses on evaluating the validity of scientific experiments by identifying confounding variables—extraneous factors that differ between groups and could explain the results, thereby undermining the researcher's causal claims.
learning_objectives: Define independent and confounding variables in the context of experimental design.
Identify differences in environment, equipment, timing, or sample selection across experimental groups.
Determine if a specific design flaw invalidates a causal claim using the Confound Check strategy.

sections.title: Understanding Variables and Validity
sections.content: In a valid experiment, researchers manipulate one independent variable (the factor intended to cause a change) while keeping all other conditions constant. If other factors vary between the groups, they become confounding variables. A confounding variable is an extraneous factor that differs between groups and can produce the observed effect, making it impossible to determine if the independent variable was truly responsible for the outcome.

sections.title: The Confound Check Strategy
sections.content:
To identify design flaws on the ACT Science section, follow these three steps: 1. Name the claimed independent variable (what the researchers intended to test). 2. List any other conditions that differed between the groups (such as environment, equipment, timing, or sample selection). 3. Evaluate whether any of those other differences could plausibly produce the measured outcome. If the answer is yes, the study is confounded.

![A flowchart showing the steps to identify a confounding variable: Identify Independent Variable, List Other Group Differences, Evaluate Plausibility, and Label as Confounded.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/a8722907-b8a1-4b04-af36-a1587486c0d1-1786506659575-239.webp)

sections.title: Common Sources of Design Flaws
sections.content: Design flaws often stem from four main areas: 1. Environment (e.g., different light levels or temperatures). 2. Equipment (e.g., using different brands of sensors or different sized containers). 3. Timing (e.g., testing one group in the morning and another at night). 4. Sample Selection (e.g., one group contains older subjects than the other).

worked_examples.question: A study compared the effectiveness of two study apps. Group A used App X in a quiet library for two hours. Group B used App Y in a noisy cafeteria for thirty minutes. Group A scored higher on a subsequent test. What is the primary design flaw?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the independent variable (App X vs. App Y). Step 2: List other differences (Location: library vs. cafeteria; Time: 2 hours vs. 30 minutes). Step 3: Evaluate plausibility. Both the quiet environment and the significantly longer study time are plausible reasons for higher scores. Therefore, the study is confounded because the app's effect cannot be isolated from the environment and time differences.

common_mistakes: Assuming the independent variable is the cause just because the data shows a difference.
Ignoring 'minor' differences in equipment or timing that could actually impact the results.
Confusing the dependent variable (the result) with a confounding variable (an unintended cause).
exam_tips: Look for words like 'only,' 'different,' or 'varied' in the description of experimental setups.
If a question asks why a conclusion is 'invalid' or 'flawed,' immediately scan the procedure for differences other than the independent variable.
Remember that randomization is the primary tool used to prevent sample selection confounds.
content.recap: A valid experiment must isolate the independent variable. If extraneous factors like timing, equipment, or environment differ between groups, they act as confounding variables that invalidate causal claims.

knowledge_claims.content: An independent variable is the specific factor that researchers deliberately manipulate or change across experimental groups.
A confounding variable is an extraneous factor that differs between groups and can produce the observed effect, undermining causal inference.
The first step in the Confound Check is to identify the claimed independent variable that researchers intended to test.
The second step in the Confound Check is to list all other conditions, such as environment or timing, that differed between the groups.
A study is considered confounded if any non-target difference between groups could plausibly explain the measured outcome.
Differences in pot size or light exposure in a plant growth study are examples of environmental confounding variables.
Testing one group in the morning and another in the evening introduces a timing confound that may affect results.
To support a causal claim, researchers must use control or randomization to ensure that only the independent variable differs between groups.
It is a mistake to assume the independent variable caused the result if other systematic differences exist between the groups.
If a design flaw is present, the researcher must reject a simple causal claim because the result could be due to the confound.
Sample selection bias occurs when the subjects in one group differ significantly (e.g., age, health) from subjects in another group.
Using different measurement instruments for different groups is a design flaw related to equipment consistency.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 3: Paper Rotor Descent
A class built paper rotors with two folded blades. Experiment 1 compared blade lengths while rotor mass was held constant. Experiment 2 added paper clips to the medium-blade rotor. Students released each rotor from the same height indoors and recorded mean descent time.

Which choice correctly identifies the independent variable(s) in the investigation?

options.C: the numerical labels printed on the graph
options.D: blade length in Experiment 1 and added mass in Experiment 2

items.explanation: Independent variables are intentionally varied or used to define treatment conditions.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 4: Stream Turbidity After Rain
A watershed team measured turbidity at an upstream forest site and a downstream roadside site before rainfall and at three times after a storm. Higher turbidity means that more suspended particles scatter light.

Which statement correctly identifies variables in the study?

options.A: The measured outcome was held constant in every trial.
options.B: No condition was intentionally varied or classified.
options.C: The graph title was the dependent variable.
options.D: Sampling site and time after rain were independent variables; turbidity was the dependent variable.

items.explanation: The correct choice distinguishes the factor varied or classified from the outcome measured.

videoLesson.title: Identify Confounding Variables in Designs
videoLesson.description: You will recognize differences in variables, equipment, timing, or sample selection across groups. Name the independent variable, list other differing conditions, and mark any plausible cause as a confound.
